passage:
Rhea: Okay, we've decided: we're going to try for one more baby!
Aunt Mira: Wonderful news! Still hoping for a girl?
Rhea: After three boys, the odds have to be on our side this time. It's basically our turn. Already looking at names.
cue: After three boys, the odds have to be on our side this time.
explanation: Rhea feels a girl is owed after three boys, but each pregnancy's odds are about the same no matter what came before. Past births don't tilt the next one.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Rhea isn't claiming one thing causes another; she's treating three independent outcomes as if they make a different one more likely.

passage: Board game night update: I have rolled exactly zero sixes in fifteen turns of Harbor Barons. Fifteen! Everyone else is building cities while I'm stuck with two roads and a sheep. The dice owe me at this point, so next round I'm going all in on the strategy that needs a six. Wish me luck.
cue: The dice owe me at this point
explanation: Jess expects her luck to even out, but each roll of the dice is independent. Fifteen turns without a six doesn't make a six any more likely on the next roll.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Jess isn't drawing a broad rule from her rolls; she expects past bad luck to push the next roll her way.

title: 41 weeks without a winner. This could be the night.
passage: Our Saturday Mega Jackpot now stands at $48,000, the biggest in our hall's history. Nobody has hit it in 41 straight weeks, which means a winner has to be coming soon. Doors open at 6, cards are $10, and the snack bar has new pizza. Come early, grab your lucky seat and be there when it finally drops!
cue: Nobody has hit it in 41 straight weeks, which means a winner has to be coming soon
explanation: The hall implies a long dry spell makes a win more likely, but each week's game is independent. Forty-one weeks without a winner doesn't raise the odds for this Saturday.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The ad doesn't claim one event causes another; it suggests a streak of losses makes a win likelier, which isn't how chance works.

title: Official says town is safe from major flooding for decades
passage: With repairs to the east levee now on schedule, Riverside's emergency manager told residents Thursday that the 2024 flood was the area's 'hundred-year flood.' Since that one has now happened, he said, another flood that size is very unlikely for several generations, and the flood insurance program can wind down.
cue: Since that one has now happened, he said, another flood that size is very unlikely for several generations
explanation: A 'hundred-year flood' has about a 1% chance in any given year, every year. Having one in 2024 doesn't use up the odds, so another could come next year.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: He isn't generalizing from a few cases; he's treating a past rare event as if it lowers the yearly chance of the next one.

passage: The forecast has said 30% chance of rain every single day this week, and we haven't had a drop. Five 'maybes' in a row that never happened. At this point today's 30% is practically guaranteed, the odds have to catch up eventually. Moving the picnic to Sunday and packing the big umbrella for work.
cue: today's 30% is practically guaranteed, the odds have to catch up eventually
explanation: Wes treats the dry days as if they make rain owed. Each day's 30% forecast is its own estimate, and rain not showing up earlier in the week doesn't push today's chance toward certainty.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Wes points to no change in the weather causing rain; he simply expects the odds to 'catch up' after a run of dry days.

passage:
Olu: Reminder that IT's random laptop compliance checks start Monday. They pick 10% of staff by lottery each quarter.
Bea: I got picked in Q1, so I'm basically safe for the rest of the year.
Olu: Must be nice. Still updating my antivirus tonight, just in case.
cue: I got picked in Q1, so I'm basically safe for the rest of the year
explanation: Bea assumes being picked once lowers her chances, but each quarter's lottery starts fresh. She has the same 10% chance as everyone else.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Bea isn't generalizing from a sample; she's assuming an earlier random pick changes the odds of the next one.

passage:
Lou: 20 cards left in the deck and none of the four aces have shown up yet.
Grace: We're not reshuffling until the deck runs out, right?
Lou: Right, so all four aces are somewhere in those 20 cards. That's a 1-in-5 shot at an ace on the next draw, way better than the 1-in-13 we started with.
cue: all four aces are somewhere in those 20 cards
explanation: Lou's odds really have changed: dealt cards aren't put back, so the four aces now sit among just 20 cards. With draws like this, history matters.

whyNot.fal_gamblers_fallacy: These draws aren't independent; without reshuffling, every card dealt changes what's left, so the odds of an ace genuinely rise.

title: Schedule pump 3 seal replacement
passage: Pump 3 has run 5,400 hours since its seals were last replaced. The manufacturer's data shows seal failure rates climb sharply after 5,000 hours of use, and our own logs show pumps 1 and 2 both failed between 5,200 and 5,800 hours. It's increasingly likely to fail soon, so I'd like to replace the seals during next week's shutdown.
cue: seal failure rates climb sharply after 5,000 hours of use
explanation: Kwame isn't saying a failure is owed by luck. Seals wear out with use, so the chance of failure genuinely rises with hours, and both the manufacturer's data and local logs back that up.

whyNot.fal_gamblers_fallacy: Wear makes each hour depend on the ones before, unlike a coin toss, so 'more likely to fail soon' is a fair reading of the data.
